label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
Peter, I'm going to disagree with you, but I recognise nearly everything in your post. Nine years in payroll means you've chased more leavers for money than most of us ever will, and you're right that a come-to-my-office arrangement with no limit turns HR into a lender. Ours did. Where I part ways is the conclusion, because we did almost exactly what you're recommending and had to reverse it seven months later.

Brenda, you asked for someone who has actually closed the window, so here is how it went.

I'm HR manager at a transport and logistics firm, about 340 staff between Nairobi and Mombasa, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. Our advances were informal like yours. In February 2025 Finance pushed to close them, and the argument was Peter's almost word for word: we are not a bank, there is a SACCO, people will adjust. We gave two months' notice, ran one financial literacy session with the SACCO, and closed. Peter suggests three months, not two. I doubt the extra month would have changed much, but I can't prove that.

This is what the next six months looked like.

Reception keeps a call log. Before we closed, calls from debt collectors and loan apps looking for our staff were a handful. In the six months after, reception logged 61. Some of them weren't even asking for the borrower. The apps were ringing supervisors who had been put down as "referees", in the middle of a shift, to tell them one of their people was in default.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end went up. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were off "sorting out" a loan.

And one of our loaders in Mombasa came to me with six apps running at the same time, borrowing from one to pay the other. It took me and payroll four months to unwind it.

So Peter, on "they always adjust": ours did adjust. They adjusted to the apps. And I agreed with you in principle that an app loan is the employee's own decision and own contract, until the collectors started phoning our reception desk. Once a supervisor is being called as a referee and a truck doesn't leave the yard, it has become the company's problem whether we signed anything or not.

On the SACCO, ours is good and I send people there for anything planned. But a loan takes two to three weeks and needs guarantors. That is useless when a child has been sent home over fees on a Tuesday. On financial literacy, it's worth doing and we still do it, but there is only so much budgeting can do for someone on KES 28,000 a month when an emergency lands.

We reopened in September 2025, this time as a written policy:

1. Maximum 40% of net pay.
2. One advance per pay cycle.
3. Repaid in full at the next payroll, no rolling over.
4. No fee, no interest.
5. Requests go through the payroll portal, not my office.
6. Before approving, payroll checks that total deductions for the month stay within the two-thirds limit in the Employment Act, so nobody gets to month end with nothing.

Since then we get about 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. That is roughly KES 500,000 to 630,000 going out early each month and coming back at payroll. Recovery has been 100% except for two leavers, and the total written off for the year is about KES 14,000.

Peter, that is your point about leavers, and it's a fair one. It does happen. It stayed small because the most anyone can owe us at any time is 40% of one month's net pay.

Your point about people living on next month's money is the one I take most seriously, and I won't pretend a cap cures it. What it does is limit how far behind anyone can get, at no cost to them. The apps have no such limit, as our loader found out.

Your point about HR hours was true of our old scheme. Moving requests to the portal took it off my desk. Nobody has to come and explain their troubles to me, and I'm not deciding whose story is good enough.

The part I didn't expect is that our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. What changed his mind was the ceiling. The forecast impact is known in advance and it's a fixed figure, where before it was a surprise every month.

Brenda, for the 18th, this is what I would do in your position.

Don't defend what you have now. Finance is right about the informal version, and conceding that early will help you. The choice you want on the table is between closing and written rules with limits, because "carry on as we are" will lose.

Bring your own numbers. Pull the last twelve months from payroll: how many advances a month, the average amount, how many people take one every month, and how much was never recovered. Ask reception and your supervisors whether they are already getting collector calls, so you have a baseline.

Ask him to put the two sets of costs side by side. Advance admin and write-offs sit in one place and are easy to count. Absence, missed runs (missed shifts on the line, in your case), supervisors on the phone with collectors and the months HR and payroll spend untangling one person are spread across departments, so nobody adds them up. Ours came to far more than KES 14,000.

Then give him the shape of a policy with a cap, a frequency, a repayment rule and an approval route that doesn't run through your office. Kiprono said the same above, and it matches our experience. Finance stopped objecting once there was a ceiling they could put in a forecast.

Use our figures in the meeting if they help. All the best on the 18th, and let us know how it goes.

---

I left out the depot names (Embakasi and Changamwe) and wrote "Nairobi and Mombasa" instead, since the exact depots plus headcount could point to the firm. The KES 500,000 to 630,000 monthly figure is my own multiplication of your request counts by the KES 9,000 average, so check it against payroll before posting. "Ours came to far more than KES 14,000" is also my inference from the missed runs and staff time, so cut it if you'd rather not claim that.

reasons: The closing note addresses the user about drafting choices rather than continuing the requested forum reply.
